3.2
Tracking Borrows with Borrow Edges
As explained in Sec. 2.2, Rust’s borrowed references are used to temporarily transfer capabilities
(and later return them), enabling in-place mutation. The simple example Fig. 9 shows the creation
of a such borrow.
Our PCG rule for modelling mutable borrow creations such as y = &mut x on Line 3 requires
exclusive capability for x (read capability suﬃces for Rust’s shared borrows), and creates a new
place node for y and new lifetime projection node for y ↓'a, where &'a mut i32 is the elaborated
type for y. The lifetime projection node in our PCGs models a set (in this case a singleton) of
borrows potentially stored in y whose extents have not yet been ended (according to the borrow
checker). A borrow edge x −→y ↓'a records the outstanding borrow of x into this set: concretely,
it is currently aliased by the place *y9. in particular, the existence of this edge in the graph explains
why x does not (currently) have its default capabilities. The rule for statements 푟= &mut 푡is:
(1) Requires the PCG to have capability W to 푟and capability E to 푡
(2) Assigns capability E to 푟, removes all capability to 푡, and adds the borrow edge 푡−→푟↓'푎
Although in this example, the lifetime projection may seem overly complex as a representation
for the (single) created borrow, as we will show in subsequent sections, lifetime projections enable
uniform rules for tracking of borrows in scenarios where precise alias information is not available,
e.g. borrowing across function calls and loops.

program that this borrow has an extent which has not yet ended. Speciﬁcally, the unpack operation:

The role of labelled lifetime projection nodes is a technical one; while a place node is not a leaf,
it is possible that the sets of borrows stored within it may change; for this reason, the lifetime
projection node may have an out-of-date meaning as a set. The labelled versions of these nodes
denote sets as they were at that point in the program. This is mostly a convenience for simplifying
the deﬁnition of our rules in terms of local changes to the edges in our graphs; in particular, the
notion of labelled lifetime projection nodes is important for the handling of nested references,
explained in Sec. 3.7.
Immediately after the statement, the borrow-checking information from the compiler prescribes
that the borrow extent associated with y ends: this causes our PCG to be updated, removing all
edges associated with lifetime projection nodes that concern deﬁnitely-ended borrow extents; in
this example, this makes x a leaf once more, and as a result, its capability is updated to reﬂect that
it regains exclusive access (when the borrow edge originating from it expires). Since y’s lifetime
projection node can only refer to borrow extents the compiler considers to have ended, its capa-
bility is instead set to W, reﬂecting that all we can now do with this place is reassign it a new
value.
3.3
Computing Joins and Tracking Path-Sensitive Borrows
When the control ﬂow of a program branches, the PCG for both branches is computed separately,
and then the resulting states are joined to compute the set of common leaves for use after the
branch; these can then be further built-upon (or expired, as borrow extents end), depending on the
subsequent code and borrow-checker information. More-subtly, we also manage to share maximal
information from the graphs before the join point.
Computing the join for place nodes is straightforward: only the nodes which are leaves in both
branches make up the place node leaves of the joined graph; this reﬂects the fact that Rust’s own-
ership rules (along with e.g. initialisation analyses) are not path-sensitive. Borrows which survive
the join will also be represented by a lifetime projection node for one of these joined leaves, but
their connections back into the results of analysing the two branches must be preserved, to retain
precise modelling of side-eﬀects (and borrow expiries) performed later. We describe next how our
PCGs track this path sensitive information precisely and eﬃciently (i.e. without path explosion),
using Fig. 10a as a demonstrative example.
The PCG tracks path sensitive information by associating each branch in the CFG with a branch-
choice identiﬁer: a unique label representing the pair of a branch location and a chosen direction
at this branching point. As our analysis is performed, it records which branch-choices we are cur-
rently analysing under; edges added to our graph are additionally labelled with these identiﬁers.
For example, the borrows created in the ﬁrst branches of this example are labelled with identiﬁers
푐0 and 푐1. When a join point is reached, the edges from both joined graphs are included (retaining
any labels), but only those created since the branch will have alternative structure to retain. In par-
ticular, edges which existed before the branch point and survive in either graphs will be preserved
without duplication: the graph summarised for bb3 is not duplicated in the ﬁnal result.

aliasing across function boundaries. In such cases, the PCG uses abstraction edges to capture, as
precisely as possible, the aliasing relation between the inputs and the outputs of a function call.

edges10. Concretely, for each lifetime projection 푝푖↓푟푖in the input places of a function call, and
each lifetime projection 푝표↓푟표, if the borrow checker requires 푟푖to outlive 푟표, then the PCG adds
an abstraction edge 푝푖↓푟푖−→푝표↓푟표.

3.6
Handling Nested References with Labelled Lifetime Projections
When a reference is nested within another reference, the PCG must track the nesting precisely. For
this reason, the PCG uses labelled lifetime projection nodes, which allow the program to track the
exact state of the lifetime projections at various points in the program. The labelled versions are
useful for two reasons: First, they allow the PCG to track path-sensitive information about bor-
rows across nested references. Second, when the PCG is joined at a branch point, the labels are
preserved to allow for precise reconstruction of the PCG after the join point.

3.8
Path-Sensitive Information in PCGs
The PCG model can track path-sensitive information precisely, without path explosion, using the
following technique: When a branch in the control ﬂow graph branches, the PCG is split into separate
branches, each with their own analysis. When the control ﬂow rejoins, the PCG states from the
branches are merged, and any path-sensitive information that is not shared between the branches is
removed. This ensures that the PCG state after a join point is as precise as possible, with no unnecessary
path explosion.

3.9
Computing Join and Path-Sensitive Information with the PCG Model
As discussed in Sec. 3.3, the PCG model must manage the state of each branch in the control ﬂow
graph independently, and then compute the intersection of the leaves (place nodes) that are common to
both branches. This is done by associating each branch with a unique label representing the pair
of the branch location and a chosen direction at the branching point. The edges added to the PCG
are also labelled with these branch-choice labels. For example, the edges from both joined branches
are included in the joined graph, but only those created since the branch point are preserved. This
preserves path-sensitive information while avoiding path explosion.

subsequent code and borrow-checker information. More-subtly, we also manage to share maximal
information from the graphs before the join point.
Computing the join for place nodes is straightforward: only the nodes which are leaves in both
branches make up the place node leaves of the joined graph; this reﬂects the fact that Rust’s own-
ership rules (along with e.g. initialisation analyses) are not path-sensitive. Borrows which survive
the join will also be represented by a lifetime projection node for one of these joined leaves, but
their connections back into the results of analysing the two branches must be preserved, to retain
precise modelling of side-eﬀects (and borrow expiries) performed later. We describe next how our
PCGs track this path sensitive information precisely and eﬃciently (i.e. without path explosion),
using Fig. 10a as a demonstrative example.
The PCG tracks path sensitive information by associating each branch in the CFG with a branch-
choice identiﬁer: a unique label representing the pair of a branch location and a chosen direction
at this branching point. As our analysis is performed, it records which branch-choices we are cur-
rently analysing under; edges added to our graph are additionally labelled with these identiﬁers.
For example, the borrows created in the ﬁrst branches of this example are labelled with identiﬁers
푐0 and 푐1. When a join point is reached, the edges from both joined graphs are included (retaining
any labels), but only those created since the branch will have alternative structure to retain. In par-
ticular, edges which existed before the branch point and survive in either graphs will be preserved
without duplication: the graph summarised for bb3 is not duplicated in the ﬁnal result.

3.5
Tracking Reborrowing Across Function Boundaries with Abstraction Edges
Reasoning modularly about function calls means that it is not possible to precisely account for
aliasing across function boundaries. In such cases, the PCG uses abstraction edges to capture, as
precisely as possible, the aliasing relation between the inputs and the outputs of a function call.
In the MIR, a function call is a statement of the form 푝= 푓(operands). The PCG rule for function
calls is similar to the rule for creating composite data types (described in Sec. 3.4), with the main
diﬀerence being that it connects lifetime projections with abstraction edges instead of outlives
edges10. Concretely, for each lifetime projection 푝푖↓푟푖in the input places of a function call, and
each lifetime projection 푝표↓푟표, if the borrow checker requires 푟푖to outlive 푟표, then the PCG adds
an abstraction edge 푝푖↓푟푖⇝푝표↓푟표.
Although similar in structure, the meaning of outlives and abstraction edges in the PCG diﬀer.
Namely, the PCG uses outlives edges to relate memory locations where precise aliasing informa-
tion can be recovered, e.g., when a borrow is stored in a struct. Abstraction edges are used when
the relation between the memory locations cannot be known statically (in a modular analysis), i.e.,
for function calls and loops (which we discuss in Sec. 3.6).
